fields.title: User flow and screen map: where the path breaks
fields.keyTakeaway: A flow is designed around user decisions, not screens. Most drop-offs live in branches that aren't drawn on mockups: empty, error, no permissions, slow loading, navigated back.
fields.checkQuestion: A dispatcher opened planning and found no available cars. What do they see, and what can they do next?
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of this node: **how is user interaction with the product structured?** We already have the objects; now comes the route along which a person interacts with them.
fields.blocks/1/subtitle: Drawn from the task, not navigation
fields.blocks/1/items/0: **Entry point**—where the person comes from and what they already know. There are usually several, and they aren't equivalent.
fields.blocks/1/items/1: **Steps and decisions**—rectangle is an action, diamond is a decision point. Each decision point must have at least two outcomes.
fields.blocks/1/items/2: **Screen states**—empty, loading, error, partial data, no permissions. This is the most valuable part of the diagram.
fields.blocks/1/items/3: **Exit**—how the path ends and where the person goes next. A dead end with no exit is a design flaw.
fields.blocks/3/text: A screen map answers "what is in the product" and is needed for completeness. A flow answers "how a person gets their job done" and is needed for quality. Substituting one for the other produces a product where everything exists and nothing gets done.
fields.blocks/3/title: Screen map and user flow are different diagrams
fields.blocks/4/text: **A cheap check.** Walk through the flow out loud as the user, naming every decision. Places where you end up saying "well, they'll figure it out somehow" are where future support tickets live.
fields.blocks/5/text: A flow diagram says nothing about how usable each step is—that is learned by observing a live person. It only guarantees that the path exists end-to-end and doesn't break anywhere.
